Job profile

Airline pilot: job profile, missions and daily life

Discover the role of an airline pilot — the missions, the daily routine, the responsibilities and the qualities needed to do the job.

The profession

What does the job of an airline pilot involve?

Being an airline pilot means safely operating a commercial aircraft within an airline. Before every flight, the pilot plans the route, analyses the weather, checks operational data and coordinates decisions with the crew.

During the flight, they monitor the aircraft’s systems, communicate with air traffic control, apply procedures and make the decisions needed to ensure the safety, punctuality and comfort of passengers.

It is a job that is both technical and human: it calls for rigour, composure, good communication and the ability to decide quickly within a tightly regulated environment.

At the controls
In charge of the flight, from departure to arrival

Daily life

A typical day for an airline pilot

A pilot’s day is far more than take-off and landing: much of the work happens before the flight — in preparation, coordination and anticipation.

{{ s.n }}

{{ s.t }}

{{ s.b }}
In the cockpit

Captain and First Officer: what’s the difference?

Entry-level role

The First Officer

The First Officer plays a full part in operating the flight. They plan the flight, fly the aircraft, communicate with air traffic control, monitor the systems and share tasks with the Captain. It is usually the first role held within an airline.

In charge of the flight

The Captain

The Captain is responsible for the aircraft, the crew, the passengers and the smooth running of the flight. They make the final decisions, particularly in unusual situations. With experience, a First Officer can progress to the role of Captain.

To better understand career progression and pay by role, see our dedicated page on airline pilot salaries. →
The reality of the job

A thrilling but demanding profession

The airline pilot profession is a dream job, but it also calls for real discipline. Hours can be irregular, nights away from home frequent depending on the airline, and responsibility remains high on every flight.

It is also a tightly regulated profession: regular training, simulator checks, medical examinations, strict procedures and continuous maintenance of skills.

The profile

The qualities you need to become an airline pilot

Being an airline pilot takes far more than technical skills. It calls for a personality suited to the responsibilities of the cockpit.

Without borders

A profession open to the world

The airline pilot profession can open the door to an international career. Depending on their licence, experience, ratings and airline needs, a pilot can work in France, Europe or other regions of the world.

Aviation English is essential: it is used in radio communications, procedures, training and the international operational environment.

Each country and airline, however, applies its own conditions: licence recognition or conversion, right to work, minimum experience, medical fitness or a type rating on a given aircraft.

To explore the sector’s prospects, see our page on airline pilot recruitment and career opportunities. →
Keys to an international career
A recognised, convertible licence
An EASA licence is a recognised foundation in many countries. Depending on the destination, a conversion or additional steps may be required.
Opportunities all over the world
Pilots can apply to airlines in Europe and other regions, depending on their experience, ratings and recruitment needs.
Conditions specific to each country
Right to work, licence recognition, experience level, type rating and language requirements vary by authority and airline.
Lifelong learning

A constantly evolving profession

Aviation is constantly evolving: new aircraft, new technologies, new procedures, cockpit digitalisation, environmental requirements and European or international regulation.

So an airline pilot must keep training regularly. Even after obtaining their licences and ratings, they undergo periodic training — particularly in the simulator — to maintain their skills and remain fit to fly.

It is a profession where the learning never stops.

To understand the European regulatory framework, see our guide to the EASA licence, the ATPL and pilot ratings. →
A calling

Why does the airline pilot profession inspire so many?

Passion, technical mastery, travel, responsibility and prospects: this is what drives thousands of young people each year to aim for the cockpit.

It is also a demanding profession, calling for discipline, motivation and a real capacity for work — but for anyone who dreams of aviation, becoming an airline pilot remains an ambitious, tangible and deeply rewarding goal.

Pay

Airline pilot salary: how much do you earn?

First Officer, Captain, early career, bonuses and progression: discover the broad pay ranges and the factors that make a pilot’s salary vary.

Key figures

How much does an airline pilot earn?

An airline pilot’s salary varies widely depending on their role, seniority, airline, aircraft type, route network, country of employment and bonuses. The figures below are indicative ranges: pay can vary significantly from one contract to another.

{{ s.tag }}
{{ s.range }}
{{ s.unit }}

{{ s.note }}

{{ salaireMention }}

Newly qualified

Salary at the start of your career

Your first salary depends mainly on the airline you join, the type of contract, the route network and the role. A first role is usually a First Officer position.

Regional or low-cost airline

≈ 3 000 – 4 500 € gross/month

A sometimes more gradual start, but with rapid experience-building depending on activity, flight hours and internal opportunities.

Major airline

≈ 4 500 – 7 500 € gross/month

A more structured starting package, often with a defined progression scale, bonuses and benefits depending on the airline.

Good to know — the first role is usually First Officer. Pay increases with seniority, flight hours, ratings and access to more complex aircraft or networks.

{{ salaireMention }}

Two ranks, two salaries

First Officer and Captain: what’s the pay difference?

First Officer · OPL

The First Officer

≈ 3 000 – 9 000 € gross/month

As a line pilot officer, the First Officer plays a full part in operating the flight alongside the Captain. The range reflects the gap between a junior First Officer, a senior one, the type of airline and the route network.

Captain · CDB

The Captain

≈ 10 000 – 20 000 € gross/month

Ultimately responsible for the aircraft, crew and passengers, the Captain earns higher pay. Access to command depends on experience, airline needs, ratings and internal progression.

The market drivers

Why is the need for pilots rising?

Pilot recruitment is driven by several factors: air traffic growth, fleet renewal, retirements, attrition and network changes. Needs vary by region, airline and type of operation.

Air traffic growth

More and more passengers travel each year, pushing airlines to recruit more pilots.

Fleet renewal and expansion

Airlines are modernising their aircraft and expanding their networks, creating new operational needs.

Retirements

A significant share of the pilots currently in post will gradually leave the profession in the years ahead.

Changing route networks

New routes, long-haul expansion, new regional bases: every network change creates new crew needs, often in new geographic areas.

Global distribution

Where will the need for pilots be greatest?

Needs vary by region. Air traffic growth, fleet renewal and retirements will support recruitment worldwide.

Guide

How to become an airline pilot?

Requirements, studies, licences, training, duration and opportunities: the complete guide to understanding how to reach the cockpit of an airline.

In brief

The journey at a glance

To become an airline pilot, you need to meet the prerequisites, choose a training route, pass the selections, obtain the required licences and ratings, then join an airline as a First Officer.

{{ b.num }}
{{ b.t }}
{{ b.b }}
The prerequisites

What are the requirements to become an airline pilot?

You don’t need any prior flying experience to start an integrated course. However, certain prerequisites are essential: a sufficient level of education, a Class 1 medical certificate, a good level of English, strong motivation and the ability to follow a demanding programme.

Video · 2 min
The prerequisites explained
Understand the requirements in 2 minutes.
{{ c.icon }}

{{ c.t }}

{{ c.b }}

{{ c.link }}→
Studies

What should you study to become an airline pilot?

There is no single route to becoming an airline pilot. Some candidates go through a private flight school, others through a selective public programme, a cadet scheme, a modular course or a career change. A scientific background can help, but success rests above all on method, consistency, English and motivation.

Key takeaway

Which A-levels to choose?

A general academic track with a scientific foundation is an advantage, but it is not the only possible path. What matters most is having the grounding needed to follow the training, pass the selections and keep up the pace.

The training routes

Which route should you choose to become an airline pilot?

Several routes lead to the cockpit. They differ in pace, entry requirements, funding, selectivity and the level of support provided.

{{ v.tag }}

{{ v.t }}

{{ v.b }}
Key takeaway

In Europe, most pilots now train at private schools, funding all or part of their course directly or through a loan. Programmes funded by an airline or a public body do exist, but they offer far fewer places and rely on specific selection processes.

The Astonfly route

With Astonfly, training is full-time (a continuous path) over 24 months, with two programmes: Ryanair Future Flyer Academy, to reach a pilot position at Ryanair on completion, or Multi Airlines, to prepare for the selection processes of other airlines.
Changing careers

Can you become a pilot after a first career?

What about career changers?

It is possible to become an airline pilot after studying or a first career. A career change is not a training route in itself: it can go through a full-time or a modular course, depending on the time available, funding, level of English, medical fitness and career plan. There is no single starting age, but age should be weighed against the length of the course, airlines’ recruitment criteria and the number of career years possible after training. A Class 1 medical examination is therefore an essential step before committing.

From application to the line

The steps to become an airline pilot

The path varies with the route chosen, but it generally follows the same main stages: check the prerequisites, choose a course, obtain the licences and pass the airline selections.

EASA regulatory framework

Licences, ratings, exams: what do you need to obtain to become an airline pilot?

Becoming an airline pilot takes more than “knowing how to fly”. The path includes theoretical exams, a professional licence, flight ratings and additional modules that gradually prepare you for the airline environment. In Europe, this path sits within the EASA regulatory framework.

{{ l.l }}

{{ l.sub }}

{{ l.d }}

For a detailed look at the European framework, see our guide to the EASA licence.

Duration

How long does it take to become an airline pilot?

The duration depends on the route chosen and the school. A full-time integrated course can allow you to complete the whole programme in around 18 to 28 months, while a modular course can spread over a longer period depending on the candidate’s pace.

Continuous path
18–28 months
Full-time integrated course

A complete, continuous programme, from theory to airline preparation.

Step by step
Variable
Modular course

Progress licence by licence, spread out at the candidate’s pace and usually without preparation for airline selections.

The Astonfly path

24 months full-time — an integrated course, from theory to preparation for airline selections.

Funding

How to fund your airline pilot training?

Airline pilot training is a major investment. The cost depends on the country, the school, the route chosen, flight hours, simulators, exams and the ratings included. It is therefore essential to plan the funding from the very start of the project.

Student or training loan

Some banks offer solutions dedicated to long vocational courses.

Instalment payment

Some schools let you pay in instalments according to the stages of the course.

Professional funding schemes

Depending on your profile, certain schemes may be available for a career change or vocational training.

At Astonfly, several options can be considered to help fund your training: a banking partnership, instalment payment and support in putting together your application, within the framework of our Qualiopi certification. See funding options →

After training

How does an airline selection usually work?

Each airline sets its own recruitment process according to its needs, fleet and internal criteria. The steps can therefore vary, but a typical selection usually includes several successive assessments.

EASA licence

The EASA licence: the European framework to become an airline pilot

Understand the European framework for pilot licences — and what it really allows, in Europe and internationally.

The basics

What is the EASA licence?

The EASA licence is the European framework that governs pilot training, exams, licences and ratings. It is based on common rules defined at European level, notably through Part-FCLthe set of European rules that define pilots’ licences and ratings., in order to harmonise training and safety standards.

Key takeaway: EASA is not a “single worldwide licence”, but a European reference framework. An EASA licence lets you work within the European framework and fly international operations that fall under it. To work under another authority — FAA, UK CAA, Transport Canada or CASA — a validation, conversion or local authorisation may be required.

{{ f.icon }}
{{ f.k }} {{ f.v }}
The pathway

What must you complete in an EASA pathway?

An EASA pathway combines theoretical exams, a professional licence, flight ratings and additional modules. The aim is to gradually prepare the pilot for the professional environment and airline requirements.

{{ p.badge }}

{{ p.t }}

{{ p.b }}
The framework’s strengths

Why train within the EASA framework?

Training within the EASA framework means following a structured pathway built on demanding European standards. It is a solid basis for building a career in Europe and a recognised foundation for many international paths.

{{ w.icon }}

{{ w.t }}

{{ w.b }}
The real difference

Flying in Europe ≠ working abroad

Flying internationally under a European operator is not the same as working under another authority. Here is what an EASA licence allows, goal by goal.

The real difference: flying internationally within the EASA framework is not the same as working for an American, British, Canadian or Australian airline.

An EASA licence can smooth some paths, but it does not automatically replace an FAA, UK CAA, Canadian or Australian licence.

Training at an ATOApproved Training Organisation: a flight school officially approved by the authority. — an Approved Training Organisation — means the school is approved to deliver training that complies with the requirements of the competent authority. It is a mark of supervision, regulatory compliance and seriousness, for students and parents alike.

Why does Qualiopi certification matter?

Astonfly is Qualiopi-certified. This certification attests that our training process meets the national quality standard and is a necessary condition for certain programmes to qualify for public or pooled funding.

Qualiopi does not, however, guarantee a course’s automatic eligibility for every scheme, nor the acceptance of a funding application. Qualiopi is mandatory for providers wishing to access funding from bodies such as OPCO, Transitions Pro, the French State, the regions, the Caisse des dépôts, France Travail or Agefiph.

What is the Ryanair programme?

Ryanair selects and audits a limited number of partner schools in Europe, then follows students throughout their training to ensure its standards are met. In France, Astonfly is the only school selected and the official partner since 2023, following an audit of its teaching, fleet and results.
You train for 24 months at Astonfly, with regular monitoring by Ryanair. A conditional job offer is signed before the programme begins: your professional goal is set from the start, subject to your success and to meeting the required conditions.

The Multi Airlines programme

What is the Multi Airlines programme?

Multi Airlines is a 24-month, full-time, English-language airline pilot programme at Astonfly. It is for candidates who want to become airline pilots while keeping the freedom to target several airlines after their training.

Home›Admissions›Class 1 medical certificate
The medical step

Class 1 medical
certificate: the health step to become an airline pilot

Before starting professional pilot training, you must obtain a Class 1 medical certificate. It checks that your health is compatible with the demands of the job.

Talk to an adviser Understand the process
Understanding the step

What is the Class 1 medical certificate?

The Class 1 medical certificate is the medical fitness required to work as a professional pilot. It is issued after an aviation medical examination carried out by an approved centre or examiner. The aim: to check that the candidate can follow pilot training and operate in an environment where safety is essential.

In short: without a valid Class 1 medical certificate, you cannot work as a professional pilot.
Why it is mandatory

An examination designed for flight safety

The Class 1 medical checks that your health is compatible with the demands of professional flying. It isn’t there to catch you out or measure your fitness level: it simply ensures you can learn and fly safely.

Key takeaway: it isn’t an athletic test. The aim is to verify medical fitness, not to select candidates on physical performance.

Airline pilot training, in detail

Discover the full Astonfly pathway: 24 months full-time, 100% in English, to learn the theory, build up your flying and prepare for airline standards.

CHOOSING YOUR PATH

Two programmes, one shared foundation

At Astonfly, the Ryanair Future Flyer Academy and Multi Airlines programmes share the same 24-month training foundation: theory, practical flying, ratings and preparation for crew work. The difference lies in the career goal and the support after training.
Ryanair Future Flyer Academy

For candidates who want to aim for Ryanair from the outset, with an airline-focused path and a conditional job offer before training.

Ryanair goal Conditional job offer Targeted airline path
Discover the programme →
Multi Airlines

For candidates who want to keep several options open and prepare for the selections of different airlines after their training.

Airline of your choice Preparation for selections Career support

YOUR JOURNEY AT A GLANCE

Your 24-month journey

Over 24 months you progress step by step: you start by learning the fundamentals of the job, then move on to practical flying and simulator work. By the end of the course, you are ready for the next stage of your path according to the programme chosen: Ryanair Future Flyer Academy or Multi Airlines. 

01
THEORY PHASE · 9 MONTHS

Learn the fundamentals through theory

You start by understanding what a pilot must know before flying in a professional environment: weather, navigation, rules of the air, flight preparation, safety, communication and how the aircraft works.

9 months of classes 13 ATPL exams Fundamentals
02
PRACTICAL PHASE · 15 MONTHS

Learn to fly, step by step

You learn to fly step by step: first your early flights and navigation, then more advanced flying such as night flight, instrument flight and multi-engine. You then continue on the simulator to work on safety, decision-making and two-pilot teamwork, just like in an airline cockpit.

15 months of practical flying Flying + simulator Step-by-step progression
03
Next steps

Prepare the next stage according to your programme

At the end of the course, what comes next depends on the programme chosen. With Ryanair Future Flyer Academy, you follow a Ryanair-focused path. With Multi Airlines, you prepare for the selections of several airlines.

Ryanair FFA Multi Airlines Airline selections

Theory training — 9 months

9 months to master airline pilot theory

After an induction week, you follow 9 months of theory, in English, to acquire all the fundamentals of the job. This knowledge is split across 13 ATPL exams + 100 KSA, grouped here into 3 main areas.

In addition
Knowledge, skills and attitudes 100 KSA

The 100 KSA (Knowledge, Skills and Attitudes) assesses, alongside the written exams, your ability to apply your knowledge like a professional pilot.

Aviation English FCL.055

One week is dedicated to Aviation English training and the exam. The required level allows you to communicate in English in a professional aviation context.

Practical training — 15 months

15 months to learn to fly

The practical training is organised into 5 progressive blocks, delivered entirely in English: basic flying, navigation, night flight, instrument flight and multi-engine, then advanced preparation on the simulator. Each block builds the skills expected of a future professional pilot.

04
04 — Paired training

Paired training: fly, observe, analyse

Each session is prepared by two students with their instructor. While one flies, the other observes from the back seat, listens to the exchanges, analyses the decisions and takes part in the debrief. The roles then swap over across the sessions.

So the student learns during their own flight, but also by actively observing their partner’s.
The learning loop

Every flight becomes a double learning experience.

Discover our teaching method →
05
05 — Pilot instructors

Instructors connected to the profession

Astonfly instructors guide students in acquiring technical skills, from basic flying to instrument flight on multi-engine aircraft.

They also pass on the working methods, rigour, communication and behaviours expected in a professional cockpit. Several of them work as airline pilots or have operational airline experience.

Operational experienceInstructors who know the line and the real expectations of airlines.
Working methodsPreparation, briefing, decision-making and debriefing worked on in every session.
Airline cultureThe standards of an operational environment, explained step by step.
Meet the training team →
Interview Instructor & Airline Pilot
06
06 — Career

A path designed for employment

Support doesn’t stop at graduation. Depending on the programme, here is what awaits you once training is over: validation then a funded type rating at Ryanair, or the maintenance of your ratings, career coaching and access to Astonjob with Multi Airlines.

Final validation by the airline

At the end of training, a final assessment confirms your ability to continue the path towards Ryanair. The job offer signed before training remains conditional.

Funded Boeing 737 type rating

After completing the programme and passing the final validation, Ryanair funds your Boeing 737 type rating, the last step before the line.

Joining as a First Officer

You join Ryanair as a First Officer on the 737, subject to passing the training to the airline’s criteria. Ryanair highlights a possible progression from cadet to Captain in 4 to 5 years, depending on its operational needs.

Discover the Ryanair programme →
Revalidation of your IR/ME rating

The IR/ME is the rating that lets you fly a multi-engine aircraft using the onboard instruments, particularly when weather conditions don’t allow flying by visual reference alone.

In the year after you finish training, Astonfly covers its revalidation to keep this rating valid and let you continue to meet the prerequisites of pilot recruitment.

12 months of follow-up with a career coach

For the 12 months after you graduate, you receive personalised support from a career coach.

This follow-up helps you organise your search, prepare your applications, better understand airlines’ expectations and move in a structured way towards your first pilot job.

Continued access to Astonjob

Astonjob is Astonfly’s pilot career and jobs platform. There you can browse vacancies posted by airlines and operators, keep your profile up to date and present your licences, ratings, flight hours and availability to recruiters.

Discover the Multi Airlines programme →

Your graduation marks the end of your training, not the end of our support.

A word from the president

Why I founded Astonfly

I founded Astonfly with a simple conviction: you don’t become an airline pilot just by learning to fly a plane. You become one by learning to be rigorous, to make decisions, to work as a team and never to stop improving.

This training is demanding. There will be moments of doubt, tiredness and sometimes failure. We will never tell you it will be easy. But we promise you will never be alone.

For more than twenty years, our teams have supported every student with the same ambition: to help them see their project through and become the pilot they dream of being.

It all starts with a desire to fly. Yours may already be the beginning of a great career.

Charles Clair
Airline pilot and founding president of Astonfly

Home›The school›Aircraft & simulators
Aircraft & simulators

An aircraft suited to every stage of your training.

From your first solo flight to crew work on the 737, you progress on aircraft and simulators chosen to build, step by step, the skills expected of a future airline pilot.

{{ a.label }}
Astonfly aircraft and simulators

24 aircraft + 5 simulators

Three aircraft types and two simulator types, each with a specific role: learning to fly, working on procedures, flying multi-engine, mastering unusual situations and discovering crew work. The resources are used according to the goal of the session, not in a fixed order.

The aircraft fleet

Training single-engine Cessna 172S Skyhawk The aircraft of flying fundamentals.
People on board 4
Avionics
Engine power 180 hp
Cruise speed 124 kts
Take-off distance 320 m
Range 680 Nm
Maximum altitude 13 000 ft
Landing distance 440 m

The single-engine on which the basics are built.

Stable, versatile and designed for learning, the Cessna 172S is the most common aircraft in the training fleet. It is where basic flying, navigation and decision-making are built.

It serves for the first feel of flying as well as flight preparation, navigation, night flight and solo flights.

Garmin G10004 seatsSingle-engine
What you learn
Flight preparation and handling Basic flying Take-offs and landings Navigation Night flight First solo flights CPL preparation
Garmin G1000 cockpit

Learn from the first hours to read, prioritise and interpret the information of a modern glass cockpit.

Paired training

Two students prepare the session with their instructor: while one flies, the other observes and analyses from the back seat.

Training twin-engine Diamond DA42 Twin Star Two engines, instrument flight and the precision of a more demanding cockpit.
People on board 4
Avionics
Engine power 2 × 168 hp
Cruise speed 150 kts
Take-off distance 745 m
Range 800 Nm
Maximum altitude 18 000 ft
Landing distance 735 m

The reference twin-engine for pilot training

The Diamond DA42 is the fleet’s twin-engine aircraft. It gives access to instrument flight, radio navigation and the skills required for multi-engine ratings.

Two engines, more parameters to manage and performance to anticipate: it is the aircraft of the most technical training sessions.

Garmin G1000Twin-engine4 seats
What you learn
Multi-engine flying Performance management Instrument flight Radio navigation Failure management Preparation for MEP and IR/ME ratings Decision-making in a more complex environment
Advanced safety — UPRT Mudry Cap 10 The aircraft dedicated to unusual situations.
People on board 2
Engine power 180 hp
Cruise speed 135 kts
Take-off distance 320 m
Range 650 Nm
Maximum altitude 16 000 ft
Landing distance 360 m

Learning to keep control in unusual situations.

The Mudry Cap 10 is the aircraft dedicated to UPRT training. Its airframe allows attitudes the other fleet aircraft don’t: students can feel them, recognise them, prevent them and recover control methodically.

2 seatsUPRT
What you work on
Recognising unusual situations Loss-of-control prevention Recovery Stress management Precise handling Fast decision-making

The aim is not to train for aerobatics, but to build essential safety reflexes.

Procedural training

FNPT II simulator
ALSIM AL250

The environment that lets you repeat each procedure until you master it.

The FNPT II simulators are used for procedures, navigation, instrument flight and managing complex situations, in both single-engine and multi-engine configurations.

Their value is repetition: a sequence can be replayed, analysed with the instructor and repeated until the method becomes a reflex.

Single-engine configurationMulti-engine configuration
What you can train
Normal procedures Radio navigation Instrument flight Flight preparation Coordination and anticipation Failure management Repeating specific situations

In the simulator, you take the time to understand before making it automatic.

AL250 virtual tour Explore the simulator in 360° →
Multi-pilot environment

FNPT II - MCC simulator
BOEING 737

The airliner cockpit and crew work.

During the APS MCC, students discover how an airliner cockpit works, how roles are shared and the methods of crew work. This phase links individual training with the operational environment of an airline.

It introduces a new logic: coordinating, communicating, standardising actions and sharing decisions.

Full-flight simulator Simulation centre in Dublin or Berlin depending on the programme
Pilot Flying

Flies the trajectory, manages the controls and the aircraft’s energy.

Pilot Monitoring

Monitors the parameters, handles the radio and checklists, and supports the conduct of the flight.

APS MCC
What you learn
Crew teamwork Task sharing Cockpit communication Multi-pilot procedures Coordination Pilot Flying / Pilot Monitoring Workload management Collective decision-making Standardisation

You no longer fly alone. You learn to make a crew work.

The Boeing 737 simulator is not a real aircraft and the APS MCC is not a type rating. The APS MCC is carried out in a simulation centre in Dublin or Berlin depending on the training programme.

Home›The school›Approvals & certifications
Approvals & certifications

Recognised standards.
A framework that protects your training.

Choosing a flight school also means checking the recognition of its training, the quality of its organisation and the clarity of its commitments. Astonfly operates within a regulated, audited framework designed to guarantee the seriousness of your journey.

{{ a.label }}
Understanding the differences

Approval, certification, maintenance and commitment: four complementary roles

These four frameworks don’t cover the same things. The EASA ATO approval authorises and governs the training: programmes, instructors, exams and teaching resources. Qualiopi certification assesses the organisation of the training, the information given to the public and the support of students. The PART-CAO approval governs the technical and regulatory upkeep of the aircraft used for flying. The SNPL ethical charter formalises, on a voluntary basis, commitments to transparency towards future pilots.

{{ c.n }}
{{ c.tag }}
{{ c.t }}

{{ c.b }}

These frameworks are complementary: none replaces the others.

Approved training organisation

Astonfly is an EASA-certified ATO

FR.ATO.0036

An ATO — Approved Training Organisation — is an organisation authorised to deliver aviation training within its scope of approval. Astonfly’s approval is granted by the French Civil Aviation Authority (DGAC), within the European regulatory framework defined by EASA — the European Union Aviation Safety Agency.

It governs, among other things, the programmes concerned, the instructors, the exams, the teaching resources and the tracking of students’ progress.

For a future pilot, this framework allows you to obtain European licences and ratings and to consider a career with operators who recognise them, subject to their own recruitment criteria and right-to-work rules.

Main titles and ratings in the course
{{ t.label }}
View the ATO approval → Understand the licences and ratings →

The recognition or conversion of a licence outside the EASA scope depends on the rules of the authority and country concerned.

European framework Licences and ratings issued under Part-FCL rules, within the framework defined at European level.
What this means for you
{{ e.t }}
Quality of training processes

Astonfly is Qualiopi-certified

Qualiopi certification attests to the quality of the processes implemented by the training organisation against the National Quality Standard. It covers, in particular, information for the public, learning objectives, support, resources and continuous improvement.

{{ q.t }}

{{ q.b }}
{{ c.n }}{{ c.t }}{{ c.d }}

Qualiopi does not replace the ATO aviation approval. It may give access to certain public or pooled funding depending on the candidate’s status, the scheme concerned and the acceptance of the application.

View the Qualiopi certificate →
A fleet maintained every day

Astontec, a PART-CAO approved maintenance centre 

Practical training relies on aircraft that are available, monitored and maintained to the applicable requirements. Astonfly relies on Astontec, its dedicated maintenance centre, approved PART-CAO — Combined Airworthiness Organisation — a European approval that allows a single organisation to manage both continuing airworthiness and maintenance of the aircraft.

This framework governs each aircraft’s maintenance programme, the tracking of due dates and the associated documentation. The technical teams work close to the school’s operations: scheduled maintenance, handling of technical work and tracking of the aircraft used by students and their instructors.

View the PART-CAO approval →
{{ t.t }}

{{ t.b }}
Expertise recognised by the manufacturers

Astontec is listed by the manufacturers of the fleet’s aircraft: an authorised Cessna facility for piston single-engines and a Diamond Aircraft service centre. A structured maintenance framework, on the aircraft types used in training.

Cessna · Textron Aviation Authorized Facility Cessna Piston scope, including the training fleet’s Cessna 172S. See the service locator ↗ Diamond Aircraft Service Center Listed service centre for Diamond aircraft, including the multi-engine DA42. See the centre map ↗
Continuity between training, operations and maintenance

The direct link between the school, flight operations and the technical teams helps create a coherent environment for students’ practical training.

A commitment to transparency
CHARTE ATO

Clearer commitments towards future pilots

Astonfly is a signatory of the ATO charter of the SNPL, the French national airline pilots’ union. This voluntary step formalises several commitments regarding candidate information, the building of the schedule and the relationship between the school and its students.

Charter signed on 2 August 2022
